A toad is a small, four-legged animal that lives both on land and in water. It belongs to a group of animals called amphibians — creatures that are born in water but grow up to spend much of their adult lives on land. The word "toad" most commonly refers to members of a family of amphibians called Bufonidae, though it is also used more loosely to describe any frog-like creature with rough, dry skin.
But Wait — Isn't a Toad Just a Frog?

This is the single most important thing to understand about toads, and it trips up many learners. Here is the honest answer: scientifically, all toads are frogs. Both belong to the same animal group (called Anura). But in everyday language, we use the word "toad" specifically for a certain kind of frog-like creature that looks and behaves differently enough from a typical frog that it earned its own name.

A useful comparison: all squares are rectangles, but not all rectangles are squares. In the same way, all toads are frogs, but not all frogs are toads.

So when scientists say "frog," they mean the entire group, which includes toads. But when most people say "frog," they mean the smooth, slimy, long-legged, jumping kind — and "toad" means the rougher, drier, stubbier kind. This everyday distinction is perfectly valid and widely understood.
What a Toad Looks Like

A toad has a short, wide, chunky body. Its skin is dry, rough, and covered in bumps that look like warts — this is the single most recognizable feature of a toad, and the easiest way to tell it apart from a typical frog. Its color is usually dull — shades of brown, grey, olive, or greenish — which helps it blend into soil, leaf litter, and ground cover.

Its legs are shorter and stockier than a frog's. This means toads crawl or take small, clunky hops rather than the big, powerful leaps frogs are known for.

Toads also have a pair of large, oval bumps just behind their eyes, one on each side of the head. These are called parotoid glands, and they are very important — more on these shortly.

Their eyes are notable too: large, often golden or copper-colored, with a horizontal pupil.
Where Toads Live

Toads are found on every continent except Antarctica. They are remarkably adaptable and can survive in forests, gardens, grasslands, deserts, and mountains — almost anywhere that is not permanently frozen or permanently underwater.

Unlike frogs, which tend to stay close to ponds and streams, toads are much more comfortable on dry land. An adult toad may wander far from water, hiding under rocks, logs, or in the soil during the day and coming out at night to hunt. However, they must return to water to reproduce, because their eggs need to be laid in water.
How Toads Behave

Toads are mostly nocturnal, meaning they are most active at night. During the day, they rest in cool, damp, sheltered spots to avoid drying out — because even though their skin is drier than a frog's, they still need moisture to survive. They absorb water through their skin rather than drinking it with their mouths.

They are carnivores, meaning they eat other animals. Their diet consists mainly of insects, slugs, worms, spiders, and any small creature they can catch. A toad hunts by sitting very still and waiting for prey to come close, then shooting out its long, sticky tongue to snatch it. They swallow their prey whole.

Toads are generally slow-moving and patient animals. They rely on stillness and camouflage to avoid being seen rather than running or jumping away from danger.
The Toad's Secret Weapon: Poison

Here is one of the most fascinating things about toads. Those bumpy parotoid glands behind their eyes are not just for show — they produce a milky, toxic substance called a bufotoxin. When a predator (such as a dog, cat, or snake) picks up a toad in its mouth, this poison is released onto the predator's tongue and mouth, causing an unpleasant burning sensation, excessive drooling, and sometimes more serious effects. This forces the predator to drop the toad and think twice before trying again.

This is why the skin of a toad is not smooth and wet like a frog's — the dryness and roughness are partly a result of these glands. The bumps people sometimes mistake for "warts" are actually clusters of these protective glands.

Importantly, toads cannot give you warts. This is a very old and completely false myth. You can handle most common toads safely, though it is always sensible to wash your hands afterward, since the mild toxins on their skin can irritate your eyes or mouth if transferred there.

Some tropical species of toad, like the cane toad, are significantly more toxic and can be genuinely dangerous to pets and humans if their poison enters the bloodstream.
The Life Cycle of a Toad

Like all amphibians, toads go through a transformation — a process called metamorphosis. Their life begins as a tiny egg laid in long chains or strings in still or slow-moving water (frog eggs, by contrast, tend to come in round clumps). These eggs hatch into tadpoles — small, legless, fish-like creatures that breathe through gills and live entirely in water.

Over several weeks, the tadpole slowly grows legs, its tail shrinks and disappears, and its gills are replaced by lungs. Eventually it crawls out of the water as a tiny toadlet — a miniature toad. From here it continues to grow until it reaches adulthood, which can take one to three years depending on the species.

Adult toads can live surprisingly long lives — commonly ten to twelve years in the wild, and up to thirty or more years in captivity.
Figurative and Informal Uses of "Toad"

Beyond the animal, "toad" is also used as an informal and mildly insulting word for a person who is considered unpleasant, repulsive, or morally disgusting. If someone calls a person "a toad," they are saying that person is offensive, slimy in character, or hard to like — much the way many people instinctively find toads physically unappealing at first glance.

This figurative use comes from the historical reputation of toads as ugly, creepy animals associated with swamps, witchcraft, and bad omens. A related word, "toadying" (acting like a toady), means to flatter someone in a servile, groveling way to gain their favour — and a "toady" is a person who does this. Interestingly, this word originally came from "toad-eater," a historical term for a charlatan's assistant who would pretend to eat a toad (considered poisonous at the time) so the charlatan could "miraculously" cure him — showing how far a person would debase themselves for their master.
Toads in Culture

Toads have a long and rich presence in human culture. In Western tradition, they were long associated with witchcraft, poison, and bad luck. In contrast, in Chinese and Japanese culture, the toad is a symbol of good fortune, wealth, and longevity — the three-legged toad (Jin Chan) is a popular good-luck charm in feng shui.

In literature and storytelling, toads are often given personality. The most famous fictional toad is probably Mr. Toad from Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows — a boastful, reckless, lovable character. Toads also appear widely in fairy tales, often as transformed princes awaiting a kiss.
A Quick Summary

A toad, in its noun form, is a rough-skinned, short-legged amphibian that spends most of its adult life on land, hunts at night, defends itself with skin toxins, and is closely related to — but distinct in common usage from — the smooth-skinned frog. Figuratively, it can also mean a repulsive or unpleasant person. It is one of the most widespread and ecologically important small animals on Earth, eating vast numbers of insects and serving as food for birds, snakes, and mammals.
